4. Thereafter, the petitioner filed Family Suit No.136 of 2018 in the Court of Assistant Judge, 12th Court, Dhaka for the custody of her two minor sons. At that time the children were 4 years 3 months and 3 years 5 months respectively. In the said family suit the petitioner submitted an application for producing the two minor sons and to submit their passports before the Family Court. The Family Court allowed the application against which Family Appeal No.69 of 2018 was filed which, after hearing, was dismissed. Challenging the decision of the appellate Court, a civil revision was filed in which on 01.07.2018 the High Court Division stayed further proceeding of Family Suit No.136 of 2018 till 30.07.2018 to give a chance for the parties to come to a compromise. However, the said order of stay was not extended, and no negotiation took place. The petitioner made several attempts to visit her two minor sons, but every time she was refused access to her minor sons. While the family suit was proceeding, respondent No.7 filed an application on 20.08.2018 for rejection of the plaint. The application was rejected on the same date. On 28.08.2018 the defendant filed an application with a prayer for staying further proceedings pending filing of an appeal. Respondent No.7 then preferred Family Appeal No.184 of 2018. Before the appeal was admitted, the Family Court passed an interim order dated 03.09.2018 allowing the mother of the children to see her children every day. However, on 06.09.2018 the defendant (father of the children) filed an application before the learned District Judge, being Transfer Miscellaneous Case No. 551 of 2018 for transfer of the family suit to another Court. This application was rejected by order dated 19.09.2018. By order dated 20.09.2018 the appellate Court directed the father of the children to produce them before the court on 08.10.2018. The mother of the children has all along claimed that in spite of the order of the Family Court to produce the children and to allow her to visit the children, she did not get any access to her minor sons and that the defendant has been filing application after application in order to frustrate the order of the court allowing her to see her children. 

 9. We note from the petitions filed before this Court that the petitioner has alleged that respondent No.7, the husband, had installed hidden CCTV camera in the room of the petitioner when she was staying at his house and he used to monitor the activities of the petitioner when she was in the room all by herself. The High Court Division also heard about respondent No.7 from the petitioner: that she was not allowed to have any kind of communication with her parents as well as others and she was not allowed to use her mobile telephone and was also kept confined to the house. As there was existing marital relationship between the petitioner and respondent No.7, the High Court Division encouraged both of them to restore their marital relationship and on this basis the petitioner's lawyer had made some suggestion to the respondent's lawyer, but this was not accepted by respondent No.7 and as a result the High Court Division without giving any opportunity for further hearing, disposed of the Rule without allowing the petitioner (mother) to have interim custody of her two minor children who had been with respondent No.7 for more than 9 months and the High Court Division also did not consider the decided cases of this Division, such as Abdul Jaill and others vs. Sharon Laily Begum Jalil, 50 DLR (AD) 55, Farhana Azad vs Samudra Ejazul Haque and others (60 DLR) 12. The petitioner thereafter attended the Family Court and the judgment of the High Court Division was placed by respondent No.7 before the Family Court who took up the matter and directed respondent No.7 to allow the petitioner to visit her minor sons in the house of respondent No.7. The petitioner was allowed to see her sons for two days and thereafter she was not allowed, which was in violation of the Court's order and on the contrary respondent No.7 submitted an application for rejection of the plaint which was rejected by the Family Court on 20.08.2018 and then respondent No.7 filed an appeal against the said order. Respondent No.7 once again filed another application for transfer of the family suit on the ground that the Court was biased for giving direction to respondent No.7 to allow the petitioner to visit her minor sons in the house of respondent No.7. 

 12. It is an obvious truth to say that for the proper and full psychosocial development of a child, the affection, care and guidance from both parents is necessary in a harmonious household. Sadly, in a case where the marriage has ended in separation or divorce, it is difficult to ensure that the child will have the company of both her/his parents. More often than not the ill-feeling between the warring parents leads each parent to poisoning the mind of the child against the other. The child is left confused and becomes aggressive against one or other of the parents. Nevertheless, it is the duty of the court to allow access to each of the parents in order to minimise the negative effects of the physical separation of the child from one or other of the parents. It should, however, be borne in mind that the access frequency and duration must be calculated keeping in focus the best interests of the child. 

 14. For example, under Mohammedan Law, the custody is given to the mother of a male child up to the age of seven years and of a female child till puberty. The case of Md. Abu Baker Siddique Vs. S.M.A Bakar and others 38 DLR (AD) 106 arose out of Guardian and Wards Act, 1890 and the boy was above seven years of age. The learned District Judge found that welfare of the boy would be best served if he was allowed to live with his mother's relations in preference to the father. The judgment of the learned District Judge was upheld up to the Appellate Division which, among other findings, held as follows: "Indeed, the principle of Islamic Law (in the instant case, the Rule of hizanat or guardianship of a minor child as stated in Hanafi School) has to be regarded, but deviation therefrom would seem permissible as the paramount consideration should be the child's welfare." 

 15. In law there are certain disqualifications which may be taken into consideration when deciding custody in favour of one or other parent. For example, the remarriage of either parent brings in a stranger to the life of a child of the first marriage. Whether the company of the stranger (stepparent) would be in the best interests of the child must be considered. It is quite common for step-parents to abuse/maltreat children from another marriage, materially, physically and emotionally, especially when they have children of their own. They then tend to act in favour of their own children to the detriment of their spouse's child from another marriage. In the case of Rumana Afrin Vs. Fakir Ashrafuddin Ahmed and others (1996) 1 BLC 517 the High Court Division held as follows: 

 "Thus, the Islamic Law of hidnat is that the mother has absolute right against the father over the minor child till she remarries. It is to be noticed that the hadith quoted above does not specifically state that the right of hidnat will cease if she remarries. The hadith indicates that the right of hidnat of the mother then will be at par with that of the father and the case of the mother versus the father is to be decided vis-a-vis the minor's welfare."

 21. In the case of Abdul Jalil and others vs. Sharon Laily Begum 50 DLR (AD) 55 the Appellate Division it was noted as follows: 

 23. Their Lordships also referred to the judicial pronouncement in the case of Md. Abu Baker Siddique Vs. S.M.A Baker and others 38 DLR (AD) 106 where it was held as follows: 

 "Courts in all these cases seem reluctant to give automatic effect to the rules of Hizanat enunciated by Islamic jurists. If circumstances existed which justified the deprivation of a party of the custody of his child to whose custody he was entitled under Muslim Law, courts did not hesitate to do so." 

 24. In the case of Abdul Jalil cited above, and the Appellate Division held that a writ petition at the instance of the mother in the form of habeas corpus is maintainable against wrongful removal of the children by the father from her custody during pendency of the Family Suit for guardianship. The Appellate Division has also held: "It is well settled that in matters concerning the custody of the minor children, the paramount consideration is the welfare of the minor and not the legal right of this and that particular party." 

 26. The Supreme Court of India in the case of Lahari Sakhamuri Vs. Sobhan Kodali, AIR 2019 SC 2881, observed that each case has to be decided on its own facts and circumstances, and that the ultimate goal which has to be kept in mind is the best interests of the child which is of utmost importance and of a paramount consideration. Their Lordships made a very poignant observation, which I quote below: 

 28. In the instant case, when the children were first brought before us, they were aged four and three years respectively. The children had been residing with their father for some time and had naturally developed a close relationship with him. However, because of the tender age of the children, we felt that their best interests demanded that they should be in the custody of their biological mother. Order was passed accordingly. However we made it a point to monitor the progress of the children by directing periodic appearance before us as well as seeking reports from the Probation Officer who was engaged by this Court to monitor the progress of the children. 

 30. In the circumstances of the case, we do not find any reason to modify our order with regard to access and custody. Therefore, in such view of the matter the application for modification is rejected.
